facts.title: Named After a New Planet
facts.text: German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth isolated a new substance from the mineral pitchblende in 1789 and named it after Uranus, the planet William Herschel had discovered just eight years earlier in 1781. Klaproth actually had an oxide, not the pure metal; pure uranium was first isolated by Eugène-Melchior Péligot in 1841 by reducing uranium tetrachloride with potassium. The naming linked the new element to the excitement of expanding the known solar system.

facts.title: The Heaviest Natural Element
facts.text: With atomic number 92, uranium is the heaviest element that occurs in significant amounts in nature. Heavier elements like plutonium and neptunium exist naturally only in vanishingly tiny traces, so uranium effectively marks the practical end of the natural periodic table. Its nucleus packs 92 protons, making it nearly 20 times denser to handle than water at about 19 grams per cubic centimetre.

facts.title: It Discovered Radioactivity
facts.text: In 1896 French physicist Henri Becquerel left uranium salts on a photographic plate in a dark drawer and found the plate fogged, revealing invisible rays coming from the uranium itself. This accidental observation was the discovery of radioactivity, a phenomenon later named and studied by Marie and Pierre Curie. Becquerel shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with the Curies for this work.

facts.title: Almost All U-238
facts.text: Natural uranium is overwhelmingly uranium-238, which makes up about 99.27 percent of every sample, while the fissile isotope uranium-235 accounts for only about 0.72 percent. Because reactors and weapons need more U-235, uranium must be enriched, a difficult process that exploits the tiny mass difference between the two isotopes. A third isotope, U-234, exists in trace amounts as a decay product of U-238.

facts.title: A Clock for the Earth
facts.text: Uranium-238 decays into lead-206 with a half-life of about 4.47 billion years, almost exactly the age of the Earth. Geologists use uranium-lead dating on minerals like zircon to measure the ages of the oldest rocks and even meteorites. This method gave the first reliable estimate of Earth's age at roughly 4.5 billion years, set by Clair Patterson in 1956.

facts.title: One Pellet, Tonnes of Coal
facts.text: A single ceramic fuel pellet of enriched uranium, about the size of a fingertip, can release energy equivalent to roughly a tonne of coal. This enormous energy density comes from nuclear fission, where splitting a U-235 nucleus liberates millions of times more energy than any chemical reaction. Today nuclear power supplies around a tenth of the world's electricity, almost all of it from uranium fuel.

facts.title: Nature's Own Reactor
facts.text: About 1.7 billion years ago in Oklo, Gabon, natural uranium deposits became concentrated enough, with groundwater as a moderator, to sustain self-regulating nuclear fission chain reactions. These natural reactors ran on and off for hundreds of thousands of years, long before humans existed. Scientists discovered them in 1972 when uranium from the site showed a strangely low U-235 content, the telltale sign it had already been fissioned.

facts.title: It Once Colored Glass
facts.text: Long before its radioactivity was understood, uranium compounds were prized for coloring glass and ceramic glazes brilliant green and yellow, sometimes called Vaseline glass for its fluorescent glow under ultraviolet light. Ancient Roman mosaics near Naples contain glass tinted yellow with uranium oxide. The practice declined in the 20th century once the metal became a strategic and regulated material.

facts.title: More Common Than Silver
facts.text: Despite its fearsome reputation, uranium is a fairly common element in the Earth's crust, present at around 2.7 parts per million, which makes it about 40 times more abundant than silver. It is found in rocks, soil, and dissolved in seawater, where the oceans hold an estimated 4 billion tonnes. The heat from uranium's slow radioactive decay, alongside thorium and potassium, helps keep the Earth's interior hot and drives plate tectonics.

facts.title: Fuel of the First Bomb
facts.text: On 6 August 1945 the bomb dropped on Hiroshima, nicknamed Little Boy, used highly enriched uranium-235 in a gun-type design that slammed two sub-critical pieces together. It was so confidently expected to work that it was used in combat without a prior test. This same fission physics, harnessed slowly and safely in reactors, also powers submarines and produces medical isotopes that diagnose and treat disease.
